newsitem.title: USA: Ford unveils electric pickup truck.
newsitem.headline: Ford unveils electric pickup truck.

text.p: Ford Motor Co, seeking to expand its share of the electric vehicle (EV) market, on Thursday unveiled a battery-powered version of its popular Ranger pickup truck.
Company executives said the truck, which will cost about $32,795, is the latest step in Ford's attempt to become a leader in EV sales.
Ross Roberts, the general manager of Ford division, said the company chose to electrify the Ranger because of the vehicle's image of durability and the strong sales climate for trucks in the U.S.
"We think there could be a bigger demand for a vehicle like Ranger, at least in the short term," Roberts told a news conference at the Los Angeles Auto Show.

John Wallace, the director of Ford's alternative fuel vehicles division, said he hopes the company will sell over 1,000 electric Rangers in 1998, primarily to electric utility and government fleets. However, he said the company had already received a "handful" of orders from customers. The truck will go into production in late 1997 at Ford's Edison, New Jersey, plant.
"It's not a mass market vehicle but it does have a good application, it's not just public relations," Wallace told Reuters at the Los Angeles Auto Show.

The electric Ranger, which took 15 years to develop, runs on a 2,000 pound lead-acid battery located between the front and rear axles. It gives the EV a driving range of 58 miles between charges and lets it accelerate from zero to 50 miles per hour in 12.5 seconds.

The battery recharges through an exterior charging station, a box which customers can install in their garage or work place. Rechargers will cost about $1,000 each, but Wallace said Ford will give the units away for free until March 31 1998.
Unlike other electric vehicles, which are offered in only a few states, Ford said it plans to offer the Ranger wherever there is customer demand.
Wallace said Ford hopes to offer a version of the Ranger with a more powerful nickel metal hydride battery, in October 1998 that will allow the vehicle to travel 100 miles between charges.
